lines.note: Narisagaru first means falling into misery or reduced circumstances. The long ſ is part of sagari, not an f to be read as an h-row consonant.

runs.text: deſcair do eſtado, &c. ¶ Item, Estar a

lines.note: Completes decline in status, then introduces the physical sense of hanging fruit. The change of sense is explicitly marked by Item.
The second gloss describes fruit hanging from a tree. Budǒga begins the grape example; the caron over o is retained.
Completes the Japanese statement about grapes hanging down. The Portuguese translation continues with the vine on the next row.

Completes 'on the vine' and gives Naricodarete aru as the corresponding expression in Cami usage. Cami occurs within Portuguese explanatory prose; the Japanese expression is retained in its visible roman type.
Nariwai is glossed as the land's yield or cultivation. The definition emphasizes agricultural produce rather than imposing the full range of modern livelihood senses.
The example says that this year's crop is good. Portuguese novidade here concerns the new harvest and is divided after nouida-.

runs.text: de, ou fruito da terra deste anno he bom.

lines.note: Completes the translation as this year's harvest or produce being good. The source's anno and the short-s convention in deste remain unchanged.

The rhetorical example asks what one will eat without farming. The printed xezumba is retained beside xezunba below: enlarged reinspection shows five vertical strokes after z, corresponding to u plus m, although one shoulder of m is weak. The final co- begins cogai, silkworm rearing.
Completes the parallel question about what one will wear without silkworm rearing. Qin is the prospective form in the question; the Portuguese cultivation verb begins at the right edge.

runs.text: tiuar a terra, & colher fruito, que comeremos,

lines.note: Completes cultivar and translates the food question: without tilling the land and gathering produce, what will we eat? The punctuation is retained as printed.

runs.text: & ſe não ſe fizer borra, que vestiremos?

lines.note: Completes the clothing question with the source's textile term borra. In the Japanese parallel it corresponds to silkworm rearing, not unrelated refuse or sediment.
Nariwataru means sound carrying across a space or resounding. The Portuguese initially describes passing with sound or a great noise.
Completes the loud-noise gloss and begins an example about a firearm's report echoing through a valley. Ta- continues tani on the next row.
Completes the valley's resounding with the gunshot. The Portuguese eſpingarda is physically divided without a visible line-end hyphen.
Completes the explanation that the valley was left reverberating. The historical doubled l in valle remains unchanged.
Narishidai is defined as according to what is possible. This is the preferred form cited under Narifôdai on the preceding page.
Completes 'according to what can be.' The source's poder is retained without replacing it with a modern expected inflection.
Nariyuku describes a condition progressively developing. The next example begins a word for great lamentation; the partly impressed mark over o is retained provisionally as the supplied caron.
The lamentation deepens day by day. The scan and the following cada dia support figotoni, higoto ni, not OCR ſigotoni; the conditional verb continues below.
Completes the conditional phrase and cites the Taiheiki, book 18. The Portuguese begins 'as his/her sadness ...'; the source has ſua, not the draft's truncated ſu-.
Completes the sadness becoming greater every day. This supplies the direct bilingual check for figotoni in the Japanese example.

Narukami is equated with ikazuchi, thunder. The enlarged scan shows a descending comma after Icazzuchi, not the draft's period. The synonym follows i, and is not a term embedded in Portuguese explanatory prose for font toggling.

runs.text: Hũa laya de taramela pera eſpantar

lines.note: Naruko is a clattering device used to frighten birds. The Portuguese taramela describes the mechanism; its purpose continues below.
Completes the bird-scaring purpose. Naruko wo kakuru illustrates setting up the device, with its Portuguese translation divided after Por.
Completes 'set up this clattering device.' This is the translation of the preceding example, not an additional headword.

runs.text: O não auer. Vſaſe em compoſição. Vt,

lines.note: Nasa denotes absence or nonexistence and is said to occur in compounds. The next example demonstrates the nominal -nasa formation.
The compound yarukatanasa concerns having no remedy or outlet, intensified by amari no. The Portuguese causal explanation begins here and continues below.
Completes 'because there is no remedy.' The gloss supports the absence interpretation of -nasa rather than treating the Japanese ending as an unrelated noun.
Nasake is compassion or affection. The example begins showing compassion to someone, with the noun itself divided after na-.
Completes nasake wo kakuru, explained as doing someone good. The alternative gloss of showing affection follows below.
Completes 'show affection to someone.' The printed separation of lhe is preserved, without introducing a modern hyphen.
Nasakenage ni is presented as an adverb meaning cruelly. The adverbial label and Portuguese explanation are italic; the alternative follows below.
Completes 'without pity,' matching the absence of nasake. The short continuation remains a distinct physical row.
Nasakenai here means cruel or pitiless. The gloss's historical sense is retained rather than replaced with a modern colloquial sense such as pathetic.
The indented nasakenasa is the corresponding abstract noun, lack of pity. The source gives no separate Portuguese gloss on this row, so none is supplied in the transcription.
The indented nasakenô is marked as the adverbial form of the preceding adjective. The downward-pointing caron is retained; no Portuguese gloss beyond Adu. is printed.
Nasubi is eggplant. The historical Portuguese spelling Biringela is preserved, without substituting a modern initial vowel.
Nasubiba is defined as short, worn, black teeth. The tilde abbreviation in Dẽtes is retained and the comparison with children's teeth continues below.

runs.text: como os de mininos que mamão. No Cami ſe

lines.note: Compares these with the teeth of nursing children, then introduces a Cami-region equivalent. Mininos and mamão are the source's spellings, not modernized forms.

Completes the regional naming statement with the printed Chiguchita fa. The unusual expression is retained from the visible type rather than forced into a conjectural modern Japanese form; fa denotes teeth in this gloss.
Nasubizane means the small grains or seeds inside an eggplant. The Portuguese diminutive Granſinhos and the grave in està remain as printed.
Completes the seed's location, then begins a comparison 'like eggplant seeds.' The Japanese genitive continues with yǒni below.
The example compares ground tea falling from a mill with eggplant seeds. The Portuguese loanword cha is visibly lowercase here, unlike the draft's Cha; it is not a roman Japanese example fragment.

runs.text: mò à maneira desta ſementeſinha de biringela.

lines.note: Completes the image of tea falling from the millstone in seed-like particles. Both graves in mò à and the historical diminutive ſementeſinha are retained.
Nata is explained as a billhook or clearing sickle. The transcription preserves the source's functional tool comparison rather than substituting a modern product name.
Natamame is identified as a kind of bean. The source gives no species-level description, and the nasal-vowel spelling feijoẽs is retained.
Natsu means summer. The first example begins natsu ni naru, entering summer, with naru divided across the row boundary.
Completes the onset of summer, then starts examples concerning its end. Curu- continues the historical verb kururu below.
Kururu, yuku, and takuru are given as alternatives for summer ending. Latin l introduces the final alternative; the original forms are not replaced by modern equivalents.
Completes the Portuguese pair of words for summer. This is a short continuation of the seasonal examples, not a separate entry.
Natsukashii is explained through longing between people who are apart. The gloss emphasizes affectionate yearning rather than only modern nostalgia for the past.
The indented natsukashisa is the corresponding abstract noun. No additional Portuguese wording is printed, and none is inserted into the canonical line.
The adverbial natsukashû is illustrated with omou, feeling longing. The carons over u and circumflex over the final o are kept distinct.
Translates the example as experiencing longing or missing someone. This completes the adjective's derivative forms before Natçugo begins.

runs.text: Bichos da ſeda que ſe produzem no

lines.note: Natsugo first means summer-bred silkworms. The scan reads ſeda as one word, correcting the draft's ſa da; the seasonal qualification follows below.

runs.text: estio pera então começarem a comer a folha, &

lines.note: The silkworms begin eating leaves in summer. The conjunction connects this feeding with silk production on the next row.

runs.text: fazer a ſeda. ¶ Item, Filho de cão, ga-

lines.note: Completes making silk, then extends the term to young animals born in summer. The divided ga- begins gato, not a Japanese word.

runs.text: to, &c. que nace no verão, ou eſtio. ¶

lines.note: Completes the summer-born animal sense and begins the contrasting Japanese harugo for spring-born creatures. Fa- follows the source's h-row romanization.

runs.text: He o bicho de ſeda que ſe gèra na pri-

lines.note: Completes harugo and defines spring-bred silkworms. The Portuguese primavera is divided after pri-, independently of the Japanese division above.

runs.text: mauera, ou filho de animal, ou paſſaro que na-

lines.note: Extends harugo to offspring of animals or birds born in spring. The final na- begins Portuguese nace, not a Japanese seasonal term.
Completes 'born in spring.' This finishes the comparison between summer-born and spring-born creatures.
Natsugiku is glossed as summer flowers of the bonina kind. The transcription retains the source's general floral comparison without supplying a modern species.

runs.text: Certa laya de feijoẽs, ou grãos

lines.note: Natsumame is a kind of bean or small pulse. Its size and summer season are specified on the following row.

runs.text: mais pequenos que vem no eſtio.

lines.note: Completes the description as smaller pulses appearing in summer. The source's unaccented vem is preserved.
Natsume is described as a small apple-like fruit. The comparison continues after the printed da-; the source's spelling is not replaced with a modern botanical name.
Completes the fruit comparison with the continuous printed nàfega, correcting OCR nà fega. The divided da-/nàfega and its grave are preserved rather than editorially expanded or normalized.

runs.text: Hum vaſo pequenino em que metẽ

lines.note: This natsume is a small vessel, distinct from the fruit entry. The relative clause explains what it holds and then describes its finish and shape.

runs.text: o Cha moido Vruxado, & feito à feição daque-

lines.note: The vessel holds powdered tea and is lacquered and shaped like the fruit. The scan restores x in Vruxado and q in daque-, correcting Vruado and dapue-; Vruxado modifies the vessel, not the tea.
Completes 'those small apple-like fruits,' explaining the vessel's name by its shape. The doubled l across daque-/llas is preserved as printed.

runs.text: Bicho do verão que voa ao der-

lines.note: Natsu no mushi is a summer insect flying around a lamp. The Portuguese derredor is divided across the physical lines.
Completes the insect's flight around a lamp, likened to a butterfly or moth. The source's comparison is retained without supplying a precise species.
Natsukeru means taming or making familiar. The second Portuguese verb, amansar, is divided at the line ending.

runs.text: ſar paßaros, animaes, & algũas vezes homẽs.

lines.note: Completes taming birds and animals, and sometimes people. The abbreviated nasal forms algũas and homẽs remain unexpanded.
Hito wo natsukuru illustrates winning over or taming a person. The source's older -kuru form is retained, with the Portuguese explanation continued below.
Completes softening or winning over someone, then begins a negative example comparing a person with a pheasant chick and a wolf pup.

runs.text: no co,l, vôcameno cono yǒni natçucare-

lines.note: Completes the two animal comparisons and begins the negative verb. The source's close co,l, and the spelling vôcameno are retained, without changing the wolf term to a modern expected form.

runs.text: Este homem não ſe domeſtica como per-

lines.note: Nu completes natsukarenu, not becoming tame. The Portuguese begins its bird comparison with per-, continued below.
Completes perdigoto, a young partridge, and a wolf pup. The Portuguese bird comparison is retained even though the Japanese qiji names a pheasant.
Natsuku is the intransitive counterpart: becoming tame or attached. The Portuguese tornar-se is divided across the physical rows.
Completes becoming tame. This short continuation finishes the verb before the following poetic plant-name entry.
Natorigusa is a poetic name equated with botan. The printed P. precedes the synonym; Botan follows i, and is therefore not marked as an embedded Portuguese-prose term.
Completes the compilers' description as large red roses, their comparison for the botan flower. The transcription does not replace it with a modern botanical description.

runs.text: Hũa certa iguaria de grãos hum pouco

lines.note: Nattô is described as a dish made from beans or pulses. The preparation continues below; the historical gloss is retained rather than replaced by a modern recipe.
The source says the pulses are lightly cooked and then put in an oven. Nat- begins nattôjiru, a soup made from them.
Completes nattôjiru, glossed as shiru made from these pulses. Xiru is embedded in Portuguese explanation and is set wholly in the visible italic type, correcting the draft's split font boundary.
Nattoku is understanding or comprehending. Its suru construction begins at the end of the row and continues below.
Completes nattoku suru, to understand or grasp. This standalone Japanese example is not marked as an embedded Portuguese-prose typeface term.
The source prefers Nantonaritomo to Natto naritomo. The two printed forms and their different spacing are preserved rather than normalized into one expression.
Defines the preceding expression as 'in whatever way it may be.' The line is a complete Portuguese continuation of the preferred-form entry.
Nawa means rope. The proverb begins by saying the rope does not cut the well-frame; the negative verb is divided after qira-.
Completes the contrast: habitual repetition, not the rope itself, cuts the well-frame. The source prints cô with a circumflex, and its translation begins here.

runs.text: o bocal do poço, mas o habito, & continuação

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies the well-mouth and attributes the wear to habit and repetition. The translation continues with the resulting notches below.

Completes the proverb with notches or wear in the well-mouth; the scan reads mòças, not the draft's broken miças. Nauauo taguru means hauling in the rope, correcting faguru. Re- continues in the separate bottom colher, provisionally classified as a catchword; repetition on f357 could not be verified.

The isolated italic colher is treated as the far-right catchword completing Re- above. Its position matches the neighboring pages' catchword slot. This classification is provisional because f0357 was not supplied and an attempted Gallica retrieval was inaccessible; repetition on the following page could not be verified. The text is fully retained under its original ID.
